```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE)
```

You have a PK model and a plan for sampling. Before the study, or before a fit that will not converge, you want
to know three things: can the parameters be determined at all, how precisely will this design estimate them, and
what would help. This page answers them for one model, in the order you would ask. All output below comes from
running the code.

## 1. Describe what is observed and what is known

pkident takes an rxode2 model with three extra pieces of information, because the answer depends on them: which
quantity is **observed** (`outputs`), how the dose enters (`doses`), and which values are **known** (`known`).

```{r}
library(pkident)

m <- pkpd_model(
  "d/dt(depot)   = -ka*depot
   d/dt(central) = ka*depot - CL/V*central
   cp            = central/V",
  outputs = "cp",                                 # the concentration is measured
  doses   = bolus_dose("depot", "F*DOSE"),        # a bolus into depot, of F x DOSE
  known   = "DOSE"                                # the dose is known; F is not
)
```

An oral one-compartment model with unknown bioavailability `F`. The dose reaching the system is `F*DOSE`, and
only `DOSE` is known.

## 2. Structure: can the parameters be determined at all?

```{r}
structural_identifiability(m)
```

```text
<pkident structural identifiability>
Decision is LOCAL (Lie derivatives at the known initial state up to order 8, checked by output sensitivities; 5 random points).
Methods agree at 5 of 5 points.
  CL           combination_only
  F            combination_only
  V            combination_only
  ka           identifiable
Identifiable combinations:
  CL/F
  CL/V
```

Read the four words:

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `identifiable` | The data can determine the parameter by itself (`ka`). |
| `combination_only` | The parameter cannot be separated, but a combination of it can (`CL`, `F`, `V`; the combinations are `CL/F` and `CL/V`). |
| `non_identifiable` | Neither the parameter nor a combination of it. |
| `unresolved` | The methods cannot decide; pkident says so instead of guessing. |

Here the concentration only ever shows `F*DOSE` through `V`, so clearance and volume are determined only
relative to `F`. No amount of sampling changes this; only a different experiment does, for example an
intravenous dose given to the same subjects, or knowing `F`. The decision is **local** (at random points of the
parameter space) and is made only when two independent methods agree: *Methods agree at 5 of 5 points*.

## 3. Make `F` known and ask again

`reference_model()` has the model with `F` known, among a set of textbook models checked against analytical
results (`reference_models()` lists them):

```{r}
a3 <- reference_model("A3")
a3
structural_identifiability(a3)
```

```text
<pkident_model>
States:      depot, central
Outputs:     cp
Parameters:  CL, V, ka
Known:       DOSE
  d/dt(depot) = -ka*depot;  depot(0) = DOSE
  d/dt(central) = ka*depot - CL*central/V;  central(0) = 0
  cp = central/V
<pkident structural identifiability>
Decision is LOCAL (Lie derivatives at the known initial state up to order 3, checked by output sensitivities; 5 random points).
Methods agree at 5 of 5 points.
  CL           identifiable
  V            identifiable
  ka           identifiable
```

All three parameters are identifiable. This is the best case: continuous, noise-free observation.
Structural identifiability says it is *possible*; it does not say your samples are enough.

## 4. Design: how precisely, with these samples?

Give the parameter values you expect, the residual error of the assay, and the sampling times.
`practical_identifiability()` returns the expected relative standard error (RSE) of each parameter from the
Fisher information:

```{r}
values <- c(ka = 1, CL = 2, V = 20, DOSE = 100)
error  <- residual_error(add = 0.05, prop = 0.1)   # additive 0.05 plus 10% proportional

practical_identifiability(a3, design = c(0.5, 1, 2), values = values, error = error)
```

```text
<pkident practical identifiability>
Expected Fisher information for 1 individual(s), 3 observations each; LOCAL (linear) approximation.
Condition number (log scale): 36900
  CL           RSE    975.1%  unresolved
  V            RSE    224.2%  unresolved
  ka           RSE    257.2%  unresolved
Note: some RSEs exceed 30%; the linear approximation is unreliable and the RSEs of all parameters may be underestimated. Examine likelihood profiles.
Weakest direction: +0.94 log(CL) -0.25 log(ka) -0.22 log(V) (expected SD on log scale 10.3)
```

Three samples in the first two hours see the absorption but hardly the elimination, so the RSE of `CL` is
975%: the parameter is determinable in principle (section 3) and not with this design. The *weakest
direction* names what the data cannot resolve here, mostly `log(CL)`. Samples out to 24 hours change that:

```{r}
practical_identifiability(a3, design = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24), values = values, error = error)
```

```text
<pkident practical identifiability>
Expected Fisher information for 1 individual(s), 8 observations each; LOCAL (linear) approximation.
Condition number (log scale): 13.3
  CL           RSE      4.7%  identifiable
  V            RSE      7.1%  identifiable
  ka           RSE     14.6%  identifiable
Weakest direction: +0.93 log(ka) +0.37 log(V) (expected SD on log scale 0.156)
```

`unresolved` here means the RSE is above the limit (30% by default, `rse_limit`); `identifiable` means below.
The numbers are a linear approximation at the values you gave; when they are above 30% treat them as a
warning, not a measurement (the note says so).

## 5. Compare candidate designs side by side

`compare_designs()` takes named candidates, each an `experiment()`: sampling times, the dose, and the number of
individuals. It adds the structural status for what each one observes:

```{r}
compare_designs(
  a3,
  candidates = list(
    early_3     = experiment(c(0.5, 1, 2), values = c(DOSE = 100)),
    full_8      = experiment(c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24), values = c(DOSE = 100)),
    early_3_x12 = experiment(c(0.5, 1, 2), values = c(DOSE = 100), n = 12)
  ),
  values = values, error = error
)
```

```text
<pkident design comparison>
Expected RSE (%) from the Fisher information; structural status for the observed outputs (LOCAL).
  parameter        early_3      full_8 early_3_x12
  CL                 975.1         4.7       281.5
  V                  224.2         7.1        64.7
  ka                 257.2        14.6        74.3
  identifiable         0/3         3/3         0/3
Practically identifiable: RSE <= 30%.
```

Twelve individuals with the early design (`early_3_x12`) bring the RSE of `CL` from 975% to 282%; one individual
with eight samples reaches 4.7%. When the design lacks late samples, more subjects do not replace them. No
design is optimised: you supply the candidates and pkident reports each.

## 6. Where to go next

- **After a fit.** `classify_profiles()` takes an nlmixr2 fit and says, per parameter, whether the likelihood
  profile is bounded, one-sided, flat or shallow, and whether that is a property of the model (compared with the
  structural result) or of the data.
- **Case studies.** [Nimotuzumab target-mediated disposition](nimotuzumab-tmdd.html),
  [PSA follow-up for regrowth](psa-regrowth.html) and
  [reference models](reference-models.html) use these functions on real questions.
- `?pkpd_model` for infusions, known input signals and PD models; `as_table()` turns any result into a data
  frame.
